attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter. He quotes Amazon's wording only to dispute it.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the factual core (not fully operational, ~250MW against 2.2GW) but leaves out the explicit charge that Amazon is lying. The contract puts that element back.

contract.note: The plain reading, that Amazon materially overstated readiness, is ordinary. Keeping the launched cluster separate from the eventual campus is fair. Requiring proof of knowledge for 'lying' follows the speaker's own word. The result depends on what 'fully operational' covers.

evidence.note: Amazon's own October 2025 statement and the wording Zitron disputes. It is a company disclosure, not an independent commissioning record. It also says the cluster spans multiple US data centers.

Independent October 2025 reporting describes 2.2GW as the eventual full-site figure, with seven buildings already online. This weakens the 2.2GW comparison but is not a commissioning record for April 2026.
Anthropic, as the customer, confirms ongoing work on Rainier in April 2026. It does not establish what scope was commissioned or operating.

reviews.rationale: The evidence leans against Zitron's inference: CNBC presents 2.2GW as a future full-site figure and reports buildings already online. But there is no independent commissioning or utility record of what was operating in April 2026, and nothing on whether Amazon knowingly misdescribed it. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own explicit prediction ('I'm making the call').

semantics.note: This is a firm forecast. The proposition keeps the majority threshold, the 'some or all customers' qualifier and the end-2026 deadline. The cost motive is rightly treated as explanation, not as a condition.

contract.note: Counting each service equally, requiring a real transition after the post, and treating token-tied credits as qualifying are all ordinary readings. Because the speaker named no population, the denominator chosen will decide the result.

evidence.note: GitHub's dated changelog confirms one service moved to credit-based billing on June 1. One service says nothing about the share across all services.
Secondary report that GitHub's credits are consumed by tokens. This supports GitHub counting as a qualifying case, but it is still only one service.
Pricing survey available October 22, before the cutoff. It is a single snapshot with many services publishing no pricing, and it does not measure transitions after April 21.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is December 31, 2026, after the evaluation date. The early-resolution rule needs documented transitions at more than half of a defined population, and the packet documents only GitHub. Not having happened yet is not failure, so the forecast cannot be scored now.

attribution.note: Zitron's own explainer in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the claim that companies 'almost always' lose money, with the light-user exception, as a statement about current subscription economics. The Opus price is correctly treated as an example.

contract.note: Asking for per-user economics, defining light use separately from profitability, and separating retail API prices from actual costs is a fair, ordinary reading of firm language.

evidence.note: Confirms the Opus 4.7 list prices Zitron cites. List prices are not actual serving costs, and this shows nothing about subscriber profitability.

Cursor's 2025 post shows extra usage could be paid for at cost, and that most Pro users stayed within their included usage. It is from a different period, a single company disclosure, and gives no margins.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no representative per-subscriber data for April 2026 matching revenue to actual serving costs. The price page and Cursor's 2025 post are context only and neither show nor refute that ordinary users are almost always unprofitable.

attribution.note: Zitron's own 'Pale Horse' line in his newsletter.

semantics.note: This is a diagnostic claim: any further price rise or degradation signals cash pressure. The proposition keeps the trigger and covers both companies.

contract.note: Reading 'a sign' as a reliable indicator and 'running low on cash' as near-term funding pressure are defensible readings, but the speaker supplied neither. A warning-sign reading would be weaker. Whether one unrelated outage counts as a qualifying degradation also depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: A late-October outage in a third-party connector, attributed to an upstream provider. At most this is evidence of the trigger, not of the claimed link to cash. It does not support the claim.

Anthropic's S-1 shows large cash at June 30, 2026. That date does not match the incident, the figure covers Anthropic only, and it is company-reported and unaudited. It cautions against assuming scarcity but is not a matched record.

reviews.rationale: No evidence ties any price or service change to cash pressure, and there is nothing at all for OpenAI. Anthropic's large June cash balance and a connector outage blamed on an upstream provider point against a cash link, but they are not matched in time and the incident is a weak example of a qualifying degradation. Neither condition is met.
